meta.title: Who really said "People Who Say It Cannot Be Done Should Not Interrupt Those Who Are Doing It"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Quote Investigator traces it to an unsigned 1902 filler in Puck magazine. Confucius never said it, and the George Bernard Shaw credit is spurious.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'People Who Say It Cannot Be Done Should Not Interrupt Those Who Are Doing It'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Confucius. The earliest known version is an unsigned 1902 filler in Puck magazine; PolitiFact rated the 'Chinese proverb' claim False.

answer.label: Not Confucius — an anonymous 1902 magazine filler
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ found “no substantive support” for the Confucius attribution, and traced the saying instead to an unsigned filler item in the American humor magazine Puck on 24 December 1902: “Things move along so rapidly nowadays that people saying: ‘It can’t be done,’ are always being interrupted by somebody doing it.” The modern wording is a much later reshaping whose author is unknown; the “Confucius say” form is first documented in March 1962, and the George Bernard Shaw credit — first documented in 2004 — is, in QI’s word, spurious.

source.excerpt: Things move along so rapidly nowadays that people saying: “It can’t be done,” are always being interrupted by somebody doing it.
trail: 24 December 1902 — Puck, New York. The earliest known version appears as an unsigned filler item on page 2. It is reprinted on 7 March 1903 by The Public of Chicago with an acknowledgement to Puck, and again in Kindergarten Magazine in April 1903. Quote Investigator ↗

May 1914 — The Philistine. Elbert Hubbard prints a variant but writes “Some one has said,” disclaiming authorship. He is credited with it anyway from 1915 onward, and still in reference works decades later ↗ — a 3 April 1915 Democrat-Forum advertisement, and Evan Esar’s Dictionary of Humorous Quotations in 1949.

March 1962 — Adult Leadership. The first documented Confucian version, in the “Confucius say: Man who…” joke format. A 1974 U.S. Senate hearing record repeats it as Confucius; a 1977 Georgia newspaper upgrades it to an “old Chinese proverb.” Chronology ↗

2004, then June 2018. The modern wording surfaces credited to George Bernard Shaw in a book about the Smithsonian. Fourteen years on it is tweeted as a “Chinese Proverb” and rated False by PolitiFact ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is the whole item — a single sentence, no byline, no context, printed to fill space. It is the earliest version Quote Investigator ↗ has located. Note what it is not: it is an observation about how fast the world is changing, not an instruction to obstructionists. The imperative form — “should not interrupt” — is not documented until 1962.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for the wording on this page. The 1902 Puck filler and its 1903 reprints are long in the public domain in the United States, but that is a different sentence. The familiar modern wording is an anonymous reshaping whose author, date and place of first composition are all unidentified — the earliest instance Quote Investigator ↗ documents is from 2004, well inside the copyright term, and even that one is a re-quotation rather than an origin. Treat it as unsourced and unclearable.

author.name: Anonymous (Puck magazine)
author.heading: Where the trail starts
author.metaLine: Puck · American humor weekly, 1876–1918 · unsigned filler item, 24 December 1902
author.bio: The line has no known author. Its earliest documented ancestor is an unsigned one-sentence filler in Puck, which Wikipedia describes ↗ as the first successful humor magazine in the United States, published from 1876 to 1918 and produced from the Puck Building in New York. Filler items of this kind were printed to fill column space, usually without a byline, and were freely reprinted by other papers — which is exactly what happened here, with The Public of Chicago picking it up on 7 March 1903 and Kindergarten Magazine in April 1903. Over the following decades the sentence was compressed, re-pointed and repeatedly re-credited, until the compact modern form arrived attached to names that never said it.

misattribution.heading: Four wrong credits, in the order they appeared
misattribution.intro: This saying has been pinned on more famous men than almost any other one-liner of its size. Quote Investigator ↗ dates each credit, and none of them reaches the 1902 original.

items.why: Hubbard printed a variant in The Philistine in May 1914 but prefaced it “Some one has said,” declining credit. A 1915 Missouri newspaper advertisement and Evan Esar’s 1949 Dictionary of Humorous Quotations credited him anyway. See the chronology ↗.

The earliest documented Confucian version appeared in the periodical Adult Leadership in March 1962, cast in the “Confucius say: Man who…” pidgin format that QI notes was long used for gags unconnected to genuine Confucian sayings. It surfaced in a 1974 U.S. Senate hearing record and has never been traced any earlier. Quote Investigator ↗.

A Marietta, Georgia newspaper called it an old Chinese proverb in October 1977; the framing spread from there. When it was tweeted as a Chinese Proverb on 11 June 2018, PolitiFact rated the claim False ↗: the Asia Society’s Isaac Stone Fish said the line cannot be reasonably attributed to anyone in the Chinese intellectual tradition, and East Asian studies professors at Princeton and Penn agreed it is not Chinese.
The familiar modern sentence first appears credited to Shaw in a 2004 book about the Smithsonian, alongside other Shaw one-liners. QI’s verdict on that link is one word: spurious. Read the entry ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The saying is American, not Chinese; it is anonymous, not Confucian; and the earliest version anyone has found is a joke about the speed of invention, printed to fill a column inch in Puck on 24 December 1902 — per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: How a filler item became a fortune cookie
lead: The sentence people share today is not a translation of anything. It is the end point of a hundred-year game of telephone that began as throwaway column filler about the pace of invention — a joke about a world moving so fast that pessimists kept getting cut off mid-sentence. Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ shows the line shedding its 1902 framing decade by decade, getting shorter and more epigrammatic, and picking up a famous name only once it was short enough to fit on a poster.

The turn that mattered came in March 1962, when a periodical called Adult Leadership printed it in the “Confucius say” pidgin-joke template — a format, QI notes, long used for gags with no connection to the genuine sayings of Confucius. The joke frame fell away and the attribution stayed. By 1977 a Georgia newspaper was calling it an old Chinese proverb, and in June 2018 it was tweeted to millions as one, prompting a PolitiFact fact-check ↗ in which a Princeton sinologist compared the habit to the old fashion of putting “Confucius said” in front of a weak joke.
context.detailsSummary: The Elbert Hubbard branch — a credit he never claimed
detailsBody: In May 1914 the aphorist Elbert Hubbard printed a variant in The Philistine: A Periodical of Protest, the magazine he edited — but he opened it with “Some one has said,” explicitly declining authorship. It did not help. A 1915 newspaper advertisement in Missouri printed a version over his name, and Evan Esar’s Dictionary of Humorous Quotations was still crediting Hubbard in 1949.

Hubbard, who founded the Roycrofters ↗ and edited The Philistine, died aboard the Lusitania in 1915 — so nearly every attribution to him was made after he could contest it. His is the one wrong credit in this story where the man himself is on record saying the line was not his.
context.pull: It was never wisdom from the East. It was a gag about the Wright brothers’ century, printed to fill a column inch.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator found no substantive support for ascribing the saying to Confucius or George Bernard Shaw; the earliest known version is an unsigned filler item in Puck, 24 December 1902, volume 52, page 2, reading "Things move along so rapidly nowadays that people saying: 'It can't be done,' are always being interrupted by somebody doing it"; it was reprinted 7 March 1903 in The Public (Chicago) and April 1903 in Kindergarten Magazine; Elbert Hubbard printed a variant in The Philistine in May 1914 prefaced "Some one has said"; a 1915 Democrat-Forum advertisement and Evan Esar's 1949 Dictionary of Humorous Quotations credited Hubbard; the "Confucius say: Man who say it cannot be done, should not interrupt man doing it" version appeared in Adult Leadership, March 1962; a 1974 U.S. Senate hearing and a 1977 Marietta Daily Journal piece repeated it as Confucius / an old Chinese proverb; and the modern wording appears credited to Shaw in a 2004 book about the Smithsonian, a linkage QI calls spurious.

PolitiFact rated False the claim that "Those who say it can not be done, should not interrupt those doing it", tweeted 11 June 2018 as a Chinese Proverb, is authentically Chinese; it cites Princeton's Willard J. Peterson comparing the framing to the old fashion of prefacing weak jokes with "Confucius said", and the Asia Society's Isaac Stone Fish saying the quote cannot be reasonably attributed to anyone in the Chinese intellectual tradition; it notes the saying first appeared in the American humor magazine Puck in 1902 and was misattributed to Confucius by 1962.

Wiktionary treats "those who say it cannot be done should not interrupt those doing it" as an English proverb, gives its etymology as possibly from a Chicago newspaper in 1903 quoting the "Things move along so rapidly nowadays..." wording, and attributes it to no ancient author (no mention of Confucius or Shaw), referencing Quote Investigator.

Wikiquote's Confucius page collects his sourced sayings along with misattributed ones, and neither "People who say it cannot be done should not interrupt those who are doing it" nor "Man who say it cannot be done should not interrupt man doing it" appears anywhere on it.

Puck was the first successful humor magazine in the United States, published from 1876 to 1918, founded by Joseph Keppler and Adolph Schwarzmann and associated with the Puck Building in New York City.

Elbert Hubbard (1856–1915) edited and published The Philistine: A Periodical of Protest, founded the Roycrofters in East Aurora, New York in 1895, and died when the RMS Lusitania was torpedoed on 7 May 1915.
